name: BBT
seoDesc: BBT: work out usual temperature check time from the actual temperature check time and the measured temperature. A free health calculator with the formula,…
summary: Give the BBT calculator the actual temperature check time, the measured temperature and the temperature difference and it returns usual temperature check time. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the BBT calculator work?
sections.html:
The BBT calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports usual temperature check time in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the actual temperature check time, the measured temperature and the temperature difference.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in hours / minutes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 28 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in Celsius. The unit chip switches it to any of the 8 supported units.

sections.title: The formula behind the BBT calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Usual temperature check time=actual temperature check time + 600 × temperature difference
Adjusted temperature=measured temperature + temperature difference
Usual temperature check time=actual temperature check time + time difference

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Actual temperature check time = 10 hrs and Temperature difference = 10 °C. The calculator returns Usual temperature check time = 12 hrs and Time difference = 2 min.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Usual temperature check time = 12 hrs and Time difference = 2 min should be roughly the size you expected from Actual temperature check time = 10 hrs and Temperature difference = 10 °C.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in hours / minutes, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Shown in Celsius, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.
  • Shown in minutes, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Time, opening in hours / minutes
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Temperature change, opening in Celsius
  • Time, opening in minutes

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The BBT calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the actual temperature check time, the measured temperature and the temperature difference — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the BBT calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns usual temperature check time, derived from the actual temperature check time, the measured temperature and the temperature difference. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the BBT calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the actual temperature check time, the measured temperature and the temperature difference, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter usual temperature check time in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Usual temperature check time opens in hours / minutes and the chip beside it offers 27 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Usual temperature check time = 12 hrs. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the BBT calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
